title: How do you solve a private equity case from start to finish, with a fully worked example?
description: The complete private equity case guide: entry price, debt, value creation, exit and returns, worked through a gym chain buyout with a money multiple and IRR.
hook: Private equity cases have a clear finish line: does the deal earn the fund the return it needs? Once you can work out a simple return, the rest of the case falls into place. Here is that calculation step by step.
body:
In this guide

  • When you will meet this case
  • The structure, and the first question to ask
  • A fully worked example with real numbers
  • The mistakes that cost candidates this case
  • Phrases to use
  • Practice prompts with model answers

When you will meet this case

Private equity: a fund buys a company to improve it and sell it in 3 to 7 years.

The structure

What return does the fund need, over how many years?
  • Is the market attractive?
    • Size and growth
    • Margins
    • Barriers to entry
  • Is the company strong?
    • Position vs competitors
    • Performance and outlook
    • Management team
  • How can we add value?
    • Grow revenue
    • Raise margins
    • Buy add-on companies
  • Can we exit well? (gives the return)
    • Who would buy it
    • Exit multiple
    • Timing

Return = equity at exit ÷ equity at entry. A fund that triples its money (a 3× multiple, or MOIC) in 6 years earns about 20% a year. No credible buyer at exit means no deal.

A fully worked example

The prompt: a fund can buy a chain of 80 gyms making £20M EBITDA (a rough measure of operating cash profit) for 8 times EBITDA. It needs about a 20% yearly return over five years.

Step 1: the entry. Price: 8 × £20M = £160M. The fund borrows 60% (£96M) and puts in £64M of its own money.

Step 2: value creation. Opening new gyms and raising prices could lift EBITDA to £30M in five years. The business also repays debt from its cash flow, say down to £60M.

Step 3: the exit. Sold at the same 8× multiple: 8 × £30M = £240M. After repaying £60M of debt, the fund gets £180M.

Step 4: the return. £180M ÷ £64M ≈ 2.8 times the money. Over five years that is about 23% a year (because 1.23 multiplied by itself five times is about 2.8). That beats the 20% target.

Step 5: test it. If EBITDA only reaches £25M, exit value is £200M, equity £140M, about 2.2× or 17% a year: below target. The deal depends on the growth plan.

Recommendation: "Yes, at 8× the deal returns about 2.8× the fund's money, around 23% a year, but only if EBITDA grows to £30M. I'd check the new-gym plan carefully and avoid paying more than 8× at entry."

The mistakes that cost candidates this case

  1. Describing the market at length and never calculating a return.
  2. Forgetting the exit: who buys it, and at what multiple.
  3. Ignoring debt, which is central to private equity returns.
  4. Not testing what happens if the growth plan falls short.

Phrases to use

Let me work out the return: equity in, equity out, and the yearly rate that connects them.
The deal clears the 20% target only if EBITDA reaches £30M, so the growth plan is the key risk.

Practise with these prompts

Should a private equity fund buy a chain of 80 gyms?

Show a model structure
  • Market: Growth, competition, low-cost vs premium; Customer churn across the industry
  • The company: Profit per gym, best vs worst; Management and membership trends
  • Value creation: New gyms, pricing, cost savings; Exit value and buyers
  • Deal and risks: Price, debt, return vs target; Leases, member churn in a downturn

Where to start: Return: can we reach the target return at this price under a sensible plan?

The trap: Describing the market at length without getting to the return.
